title: From Automation to Co-Creation
content:
A Product Leader's Journey Across Scales

There is a particular kind of learning that comes from working across organisations of radically different sizes — from startups to global corporations, from scrappy digital health ventures to legacy telecoms groups. The patterns that emerge are not about scale per se, but about the relationship between what an organisation says it wants and what its structure actually allows it to do. Working across companies like Koa Health, Telefónica, O2, the Financial Times, and the British Council — while collaborating with institutions like Harvard Medical School, the Royal College of Art, and Imperial College — produces a view of innovation that is less romantic and more structural than most.

Most recently, heading the product team at Sinus, a company focused on making real estate management more efficient, has provided a particularly concentrated lesson in what AI can and cannot do — and what good UX design looks like when AI is involved. The temptation to treat AI as a magic solution is powerful and understandable. The reality is more interesting and more demanding.

The Hidden Complexity Behind Real Estate

Real estate is easy to misread from the outside. The visible part — the estate agent showing houses, the sign in the garden, the property listings — obscures a much larger operational reality. Behind every transaction sits a network of lawyers, notaries, financial analysts, and compliance officers, all working with documents that exist in dozens of formats across dozens of locations: email inboxes, Google Drive folders, WhatsApp threads, government portals, physical filing cabinets, and USB sticks left in offices.

One customer put it memorably: "We have a folder culture. We meticulously create folders, organise them really properly, and we've been doing that for years." The result is information that sits inert — unanalysed, unconnected, unused. A modest pile of a thousand documents, at fifteen minutes each to read and extract key data, represents one and a half months of concentrated work for a human analyst. That is before the neighbour who double-checks the work, or the risk of getting something wrong: a regulatory fine, an incorrect rent calculation, an audit failure, or, in other sectors like healthcare, something far more serious.

From Automation to Co-Creation: What AI Is Actually Good At

The obvious answer to the document problem is AI. The honest answer is: it depends on which problem. AI is genuinely excellent at a specific class of tasks — repeated, bounded operations that a human could perform in a few seconds but that need to be performed millions of times. It is also excellent at analysing large volumes of text, extracting structured data from unstructured sources, and generating coherent drafts of images, code, and written content.

What AI is not good at — and what practitioners need to be clearer about — is nuanced legal and regulatory analysis. A Stanford Human-Computer Interaction study found that AI gets the answer wrong in roughly one in six benchmark legal queries. A growing body of documented court cases records the consequences when lawyers have relied on AI-generated citations that turned out not to exist. At Sinus, testing the AI's ability to interpret Dutch rent regulation produced a revealing result: half the answers were wrong, and customers had no reliable way to know which half. The outcome was not increased confidence in the platform; it was decreased trust in everything the platform did. The AI was removed from that feature.

The more useful frame is co-creation rather than automation. The goal is not to replace human judgment with AI, but to design systems in which AI handles the high-volume, low-ambiguity work — document extraction, rule application, pattern detection — while humans retain meaningful oversight of the decisions that carry real risk. Appropriate reliance means helping users understand what the AI is doing, where it is confident, and where it is not. That is a UX problem as much as a machine learning problem.

Designing for Appropriate Reliance

The customer who tested Sinus's rent calculation tool and then compared the result to ChatGPT illustrates a pattern that UX designers working with AI will encounter repeatedly. Users treat AI outputs as ground truth, not as probabilistic estimates. This is not irrationality — it is a reasonable response to tools that sound authoritative and rarely flag their own uncertainty. The design implication is significant: if you do not actively signal confidence levels, users will assume confidence where none exists.

Designing for appropriate reliance means making the AI's reasoning visible, its sources traceable, and its limitations explicit. It means resisting the temptation to present a smooth interface over a model that is uncertain. And it means building feedback loops that allow users to correct errors, so that the system improves over time rather than compounding mistakes. These are not features to be added at the end of a development cycle. They are foundational to whether an AI-assisted product can be trusted.

Where UX Has the Most to Contribute

The deepest contribution that UX design makes to AI products is not visual — it is conceptual. It is the discipline of asking, before building: what problem are we actually trying to solve? What do users genuinely want? And is this the best way to give it to them? At Sinus, the answer to those questions turned out to be three things: save time, avoid mistakes, and keep improving. Eliminating manual form-filling. Automating document review. Flagging regulatory non-compliance before it becomes a liability. Helping estate agents understand what they could do better.

None of these required AI to pretend to be smarter than it is. They required AI to do what it is actually good at — processing high volumes of structured data quickly and reliably — while keeping the human in the loop for the decisions that matter. That is the shift from automation to co-creation: not a technology choice, but a design philosophy. UX does not just make AI easier to use. Done well, it determines whether AI is used for the right things in the first place.
